questions.q: How does boosting differ from a random forest?
options: It grows many independent deep trees and averages them
It grows shallow trees one after another, each fitted to the errors of the ensemble so far
It trains a single very deep tree
It removes features until only one is left
questions.explain: Boosting is sequential and error-correcting; a random forest grows independent trees in parallel and averages them.

questions.q: In gradient boosting with squared error, what is each new tree trained to predict?
options: The original target values
The feature means
The residuals: actual value minus the current ensemble prediction
A random subset of the rows
questions.explain: For squared error the residual is the negative gradient of the loss, so each tree is fitted to the residuals.

questions.q: What does the learning rate control?
options: How many rows each tree sees
How large a fraction of each new tree's output is added to the prediction
The maximum depth of each tree
How fast the code runs on the CPU
questions.explain: The learning rate scales each tree's contribution. Smaller steps generalize better but require more trees.

questions.q: Which statement about the number of trees is correct for gradient boosting?
options: More trees can never hurt, exactly as in a random forest
The number of trees has no effect on the fit
Fewer trees always overfit
Too many trees can overfit, so the count must be chosen using validation data
questions.explain: Boosting keeps chasing residuals, including noise, so unlike a forest it can overfit as trees are added.

questions.q: Which kind of tree do boosting methods typically use as their building block?
options: Shallow trees, often depth 3 to 6
Very deep, fully grown trees
Single-node stumps only, never anything deeper
Trees are never used in boosting
questions.explain: Boosting builds a strong model from many weak, shallow learners.
